title: Don't Lose Focus: Activation Steering via Key-Orthogonal Projections
claim: Adding a steering vector to queries shifts attention mass away from a few important tokens toward tail tokens, harming utility.
layout: 2 stacked bar panels left, attention-head diagram right; red rerouting arrow
description: The figure has two stacked bar-chart panels on the left. The top panel is titled "Baseline Attention". It shows a skewed distribution of blue bars, with a callout reading "80% mass on < 20% tokens". The bottom panel is titled "Activation Steering". Its bars are a mix of blue and red, and a red curved arrow runs from the focus-set bars to the tail bars. A callout in red italics reads "Attention reroutes!". The bottom panel is labeled with "Focus Set (H)" and "Tail Set (L)" on its x-axis. Next to each panel is a vertical softmax heatmap strip, blue for baseline and red-tinted for steered. On the right, a dashed box labeled "Attention Head (l,h)" shows q_i and k_j feeding a multiplication node. A second q_i is added to λ r_q, which is labeled "steering vector" and shown in a yellow box. Arrows connect the head to the score strips. The eye goes first to the red arrow and the contrast between blue and red bars.
caption: Attention rerouting due to query-space steering, a key contributor to the trade-off between steering efficacy and utility preservation.
abstract: Activation steering controls LLM behaviour towards target behaviour by intervening in internal representations, yet it often degrades reasoning and retrieval performance. We argue that a primary cause of this trade-off is attention rerouting: steering vectors alter query-key matching, shifting attention away from contextually important tokens toward less informative ones. To address this, we propose Steering via Key-Orthogonal Projections (SKOP), a steering method that constrains harmful attention rerouting without eliminating steering efficacy. SKOP achieves this by preserving attention patterns on a small set of focus tokens the model relies on for reasoning and retrieval, while allowing redistribution among less critical tail tokens. Across multiple steering benchmarks, we show that SKOP achieves the best joint steering-utility trade-off, reducing utility degradation by 5-7x while retaining over 95% of vanilla steering efficacy. Our results further suggest that, in long-context retrieval settings where vanilla steering approaches are ineffective, SKOP can maintain robust performance by avoiding attention rerouting.
